projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Albert Boehnlein was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War Two veteran Albert J. Boehnlein. Mr. Boehnlein served in the US Army 78th Division, 309th Regiment. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was sergeant. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Boehnlein's home in Middlefield, Ohio on September 19th, 2001. Al was 81 at the time of this recording. When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: I went into the service February the 4th of 1941.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you sign up?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Drafted?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: I was selected by my local friends and neighbors, drafted. And I went to Camp Perry where I was inducted. From Camp Perry I was sent to Camp Wheeler in Macon, Georgia for basic. After basic we were sent up to the east coast to Salisbury, Maryland to the EDC, which was known as the Eastern Defense Command. And I was there for a matter of a year or so. And I was transferred. I requested a transfer and was granted such to join the Air Force Cadet Program at which time we were sent to Albright College in Reading, Pennsylvania for our pre, pre flights, and that was a short program of five months. And we were -- we were graduated from there and all set to go to Santa Ana, California for pre flight when the word came through that all prior ground force personnel from the Cadet Program and the AFCP were going to be reverted back to the ground forces without prejudice for the convenience of the government.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did that word come down?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: That came down in 1944. So from that time on--no, I think it was in '43 that come because then we went back to--they shipped us to Camp Pickett, Virginia, and we were in the 78th Infantry Division. And we stayed in there and I was in heavy weapons company. And I went across to--on the advance party. There is a place in here somewhere. We went to--at any rate, I went--I went oversees with the advance party for the division. And, yeah, there it is right here. For the division we landed in--we crossed on the--on the-- unescorted on the Aquitania, which was a British liner. We were three days, half days going across. Landed at Firth of Clyde in Scotland. Put on a train, the Scottish Flyer, for Southampton, England. We were shipped immediately across the Channel to make provisions for the division. However, when we landed at Utah Beach, confusion was so bad and there was nothing available to take care of the division. So they said we would have to wait a little later until they took Le Harve. So they shipped us--we waited until Cherbourg was taken, and they shipped us back to England where we were billeted at the Linden Hall Hydro which was in Bournemouth, England known as the Atlantic City of England. We stayed there until the division come over and we were there an additional 30 days and we were sent back across the Channel and we were one of the first ships to arrive in Le Harve.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: After it was taken. From there we proceeded as a division up through Luxembourg and into Tongeren, Belgium, and that's where we were mobilized to start our combat. We started--went through the Siegfried Line. We were one of the first divisions to pierce the Siegfried line. And we went through the Tunnel of Lammersdorf, Aachen. And our first objectives were Vikareth (ph), Simmerath, and Kesternich. Kesternich was the--the real battle of the whole bunch. And from there our job was to pierce the--go through the Hurtgen Forest and take Schwammenaul Dam which was on the Roer River and it was a must to take the dam so that they wouldn't-- Germans couldn't blow the dam and flood out the lower section preventing Patton from coming in from the south. So we went through the Hurtgen Forest and it was a blood bath. The 28th Division had lost almost their entire division. And to be real honest, we never should have went through the forest in the first place. We should have surrounded it, what Patton wanted to do, and cut it off, cut the Germans off but, no, we went through the middle. We got through there, captured the dam. I was injured at the dam. I was a reconnaissance sergeant at the time. And my buddy and I were to go to the base of the dam or in the area of the dam to find out where the big guns were being fired from across the Roer River and we got hit by German grenades. We were taken back and I went to Liege to the hospital. My buddy went to Paris because he was much worse off than I was. I was protected, thank God, with a SCR 400 radio on my back or I might not be here today. From that point on I never saw my friend after that. He was to come back later than I did and we were transferred to other units but still in the same position. From the dam we crossed the Cologne Plains. And our guy-- we were involved incidentally at the Battle of the Bulge, too. We were on the north corridor on Monschau and they crossed the Cologne Plains and our next objective, of course, was the Rhein River. We got down, come down from the north on the west bank of the Rhein, and to our surprise the bridge was still intact at Remagen. We got orders to cross the bridge at any cost and whatever you do, you don't give up. So we crossed the bridge. It was a rainy night, a horrible, miserable night. They planked the railroad tracks so just loose plank. We drove our vehicles across and it was a total chaos of confusion, bumper-to-bumper vehicles. Any man that could walk was on his way. Got on the other bank to hold the bridge head until we could get enforcements over there to help us. There was a tunnel on the other side with the tracks and all the Germans had moved back in the tunnel. The bridge was badly busted up on the west side from where a bomb had hit. The Germans tried to blow it, but their explosives were not effective due to various conditions, old, poor connections. So we managed--our engineers managed to cut off all of the electrical connections so they couldn't blow the bridge. We captured a group that was in the tunnel. And our next objective after about a week and a half was to move north. We moved north and northeast, cut off the autobahn so that the Germans couldn't use it for transporting troops and material. And our final objective was the Ruhr Valley which was Wuppertal and we did in Wuppertal what we should have done in Hurtgen Forest. We surrounded the whole valley and cut the Germans off and that was our final conclusion of our division. We had 128 consecutive days in combat. And from there I moved to--our unit moved to a little town of Helmershausen in Laskrist (ph) Hofgeismar. And that's where we were billeted for another 30 days at which time they decided that our unit would be sent to Berlin for occupation. And I had far more the points that I needed for being married and time in service and foreign service to come home on points. And at that point I was shipped to Camp Lucky Strike and October the 15th of '45, why I was headed home. Went to-- arrived in New York, kissed the ground as all the rest of us did. I was shipped to--where was it in Pennsylvania? Harrisburg. Got a partial pay and sent home and went back five days later and was discharged. That ended my military career.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any specific memories of Hurtgen Forest?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Oh, I got lots of them. It was truly the--the worst of anything I have ever seen. To begin with, it's almost impossible to explain what Hurtgen Forest really is. It's dark, huge trees, pine boughs clear to the--and it actually was night under the trees. It never dried up because there never was any sun could get through there. There were trails going through it, fire breaks cut in it. And Hurtgen Forest was loaded with mine fields and pill boxes. And their pill boxes were designed so that they all had cross-fire with each other because it was--it was the--the last defense they had of their homeland, that, and the--and the dragon teeth. The Sigfried Line, that was horrible. We finally--we finally got wise. You couldn't blow the dragon teeth out. They were in too deep. So we started filling it with bulldozers and then drove over them. That's the only way we got over them. The Germans had put roadblocks up. They would have explosive on trees and drop the trees so that they were entangled with each other. That there was just no way you could move them without equipment. They had everything lined up. And then Kesternich was probably the toughest battle of the bunch in there along with Schmidt, the Schmidt Barracks area. That's where the SS troopers trained and they--the SS troopers, there was no such thing as humanitarians. They didn't know what it was to be human. They'd jab their own mother. And then, of course, the dam. They wanted to fight us. No way did they want us to have the dam because as I say the dam was their last resort. If they could have blown that dam we'd have never got in there because it would have flooded everything below us and wiped Patton right out because Patton was crossing from the bottom. So we had to get the dam before they blew it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And where specifically was that dam?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: That was--the dam was on the Roer River.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On the Roer River.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: The Roer River. That was after the--after the Hurtgen Forest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that was Kesternich, the dam. What was the name of the town near that dam? That was near the SS barracks is that--

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Yes, that was near Schmidt. Yeah. That was following Schmidt, yeah. There would be the dam and we were the--we were the--the 109th. 309th. This was our job. We came from over around here and came down on the dam from here. But you can see what would happen if they would have blown that dam it would have really flooded this whole area down below there or the other way I should say.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they ever explain why the Hurtgen Forest campaign happened like that? What was their reasoning?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: What was the reasoning? The blame for the--the last paragraph tells it all. Generals, smart ass generals. Eisenhower hated Montgomery's guts because he--in fact, Montgomery when--this is a known fact in medical or in military records. When we got to Hurtgen or to--to Remagen, the bridge was intact. We wanted to cross it and Ike told Montgomery he was supposed to have gone way ahead and Ike--and Montgomery was holding back, holding back. And that used to burn Eisenhower up because Eisenhower and Patton saw eye to eye. The best defense is an offense. Hit 'em while they're running and don't let 'em stop. Well, he--it wasn't in the records. Everything had to be British. It had to be in the writing to do it. And that's when Eisenhower said cross that bridge and put every man and every vehicle over there you can get as fast as you can get it and the hell with the records. That's what we did. But there was a lot of problems because of that. That goes back to the forest. They wouldn't listen and you didn't have an officer that would go up to the front line and really see what the hell was going. That's what I admired about Patton. Now, my--I have relatives that were in Patton's outfit. They hated Patton's guts because he was a bull but there's one thing you can't deny. Patton was never in the last tank or wasn't ten miles back. Patton wanted to be in the first tank. He led his men. He didn't push them. And they--our guys always had a lot of respect for him for that. Sure, he drove them but we were fighting a war. This is what it's all about. If you're going to sit back in a hole in the ground. Like we said if we were in those pill poxes we would have lost the war because we never would have got out of them. Hell, that's protection, boy. So there we go. So it's--war is hell. There was a lot of good of it. This picture I just showed you on the last day that I left there, those people over there had a big party for me, believe it or not. The burgemeister's name was Vedderlein and he asked me what my name was one day when I was uptown and I said Boehnlein. And he says Boehnlein? He says das is Deutsch, ja and I said ja, it is and we were the best friends from there on. And like he said I had nothing against and you had nothing against me. Why should we be fighting each other. And there's a lot to be said about that. Our unit still gets together. We go down to Kaiser, West Virginia every spring of the year for what they call an Ed Kelly Day. Ed Kelly stayed at his post and he was the first one of our outfit to get the Medal of Honor. He was shot all to hell and he wouldn't go back for medical attention and stayed there until he finally got the machine gun nest and eliminated the machine gun nest. And we go to his grave in Keyser, West Virginia every--the 12th of April every year our unit goes down there and they have a grave site service. We go in there to Kaiser. People--we don't pay for a thing. They take care of everything. That's the kind of people they are. Because they still respect that what we did for their own. They had more young people from a small town in service than any other country or any other city or town in the United States. And they--their losses were horrible.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of the Bulge that you can share?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Cold. You better believe it. The Bulge was hell. Where ever you went it was snow and ice. You were wet. Memories of my first day in combat is probably the scariest time of anybody's life. You might have been in training in the States and heard artillery fire or anything else, but when you're over there and you know they're shooting at you. We were going up a little draw, going into the beginning of the forest. At that point our first--we got the first taste of German artillery shells blast hitting in the field right next to us and we all made a dash into the ditch. The ditch was ice cold water, snow up to your ass. It was--it was miserable but you were scared. The old man come back, the captain, he said come on, get up here and walk. He said you want to stand up and die like a man and stand up or you want to lay on your belly and cry. Boom. Sympathy was not there. So you ended up getting back up. From that time on I swear to God I was wet and cold the rest of the war. But we finally made it into Simmerath was the first town we hit. A lot of fires were going on there because barns, houses were burning from the artillery fire. We didn't run into any German civilian population until we crossed the Rhein. We started seeing some on the Cologne Plains going across the planes, but the German people have moved inland because we would never get there. We couldn't possibly impregnate the Sigfried Line. No way. Hitler had them all bullshitted but we did. The Hurtgen Forest part was horrible in that you couldn't get tanks in there. The trees were too dense. Mud, God, mud up to your hind end all the time. Sleep. We went for two, three weeks many times without a hot meal because the kitchen couldn't keep up with you, this kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you got in front and encountered the German people, you mentioned the one nice guy, but were they mostly understanding or were they afraid?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Most Germans--a lot of them were afraid. They'd oh, nein, nein, nein, nein, and they'd hold a white flag, anything. They were afraid of being shot. And what they found out we weren't such bad guys after all. What--what got us most that towards the end of the war when they knew they were whipped, you used to get kids, young kids, and God, our heart would go out to those kids. We'd give them half of our mess gear, half of our chow when we were in the chow line. In fact, my neighbors live next door. They are two Germans. In fact, they just left to go back to Germany today. Her youngest sister that's going back with her was just a three-year-old girl when the war was on, and the stories she told how they used to take the garbage cans, sift through the garbage cans when we got through just to get something to eat. And she said they were so grateful for the American soldiers because we gave them so much and we weren't the villains that they were taught that we were. Typical of what you got today with terrorism.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Does anything come to mind as your most vivid memory or experience over there?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: There's--there's nothing and there's no thing that you can do at home or prior to it to give you the true depth of your feelings of dying. Nobody wants to die. And yet you knew but as war progressed and as you went along and some of the things that were outstanding in my mind, for example, we were the first group over there to have a contingent of black people who volunteered from the quarter master to front line duty. I--I had a squad and I had a couple of southern boys. One from Alabama in particular and I had a lieutenant from Tennessee. And I don't have to tell you what the feeling was between black and white. Oh, God. I swear to God I had to watch them all the time because they would have shot these poor kids and yet these colored boys were terrific troops. And when we started through Hurtgen Forest, Mike was the name of one of them that I was very familiar with. He got hit. He was laying in the ditch and I'll never forget this as long as I live. And I stopped. I says Mike, can I help you. I says there's a medic, he'll be right up here, which I had talked to the medic because I knew he had been hit. And he says just remember one thing, Sarge. He says our blood is just as red as yours, isn't it? I have never forgot that and I never will. How true. We go by the color of skin but his blood is just as red as ours. So those were some of the things but the conditions. Weather. Weather was the big thing. Geez, we didn't have boots when we first got over there. We had just plain shoes. We didn't have boots. Most were throwing the damn overcoats away because they were so cumbersome. How do you carry that in a pack and a rifle? Jesus, and snow up to your rear end. This kind of stuff. You didn't know what a bed was. And then when it came to the Bulge and they hit us with that counterattack. Oh, Jesus, that was so unexpected and it blew our minds because we had--we had--the biggest thing we were to do was to clean up our weapons and get things in shape and this was--we were more or less a little on the relaxed side and wham, they hit us with a bang. And being a forward observer I had a terrific guy with me, and I certainly would like to mention his name and that is George Ellerd. George got a field commission. In fact, we're going to meet George next Tuesday for dinner. We still get together once a month. He got a battlefield commission and I was his radio operator. And whenever they wanted somebody to go out to find out where it was, why, that was--that was our duty. So that's how we got together. George was one terrific guy. He's one officer that you had respect for. He came up the hard way and he never let bars interfere with friendship with a non com. Forget it. He--he didn't go for that discrimination. The lieutenant, I don't talk to the enlisted men. Not him. He's the guy when he got his liquor, come on, let's go get a bottle and settle down, that kind of a guy. And I respect him to this day for that. And as I say we--we still get together. It's great. Many times we--when we went to the dam where we got hit we had to go down this road and it swirled around and just as you come around a bend we could see where that big 88 was firing from on the other side of the river and so that's where we set it up. And how we got hit, we didn't realize it. We went down there. That over on top of this bluff here the Germans were sitting on top here. And I had a 15-foot what they called a whip antenna on the radio so I put that on so that we could get back to our commanding officers. So we got around here and we sat down in this curve, this area here and the dam was over here. And all of a sudden the Germans must have picked up the antenna and knew we were there and they throw potato mashers over the bank. And that's what caught both of us, the potato mashers. Those were German grenades with a handle on them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's where you got hurt?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: That's where we got the hell blown out of us. George's back was all tore to hell. And my buddies with a Jeep knew we weren't coming back. They didn't--they didn't--they were waiting for us before they got too far down with the Jeep. And when they find out--found out that we should have been back and we weren't, they started looking for us. And they found us and got us back on the Jeep and took us up to the aid station and that's where we got sent back to the hospital. But the Bulge was a bitch and then the weather prohibited the airplanes, the Air Force from coming over. So we were on our own. But everything was getting short. There was no help. It's foggy, colder than hell. And finally the weather broke one day and that's the day I'll never forget. You looked up and see 1,000 airplanes in the air going over. Oh, God, what a relief that was. That was it. The other experience that was weird, the very ship which was a liberty ship that took us into Le Harve on our second trip across the Channel, hit a mine going out of the Channel and sunk right off the harbor after we were off of it. The English people, they loved us. They wanted everything we had to give them, too. Food, chocolate, cigarettes. So that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't know if I am confusing some information, but is there some kind of a story about a mine field?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Well--oh, yeah, there sure was. There is--I think it's in here. There is the mine field.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why don't you go ahead and either read this or tell this story.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: We were there--and mines are another thing. Mines are as bad as if not worse than artillery. Artillery you can hear them and you know whether they're coming in or going out. You know whether it's foreign or whether it's ours. There was just something about it and the bigger the shell, the slower the sound. You know, pluf, pluf, pluf, pluf (ph). 88s were the worst because they were a high-velocity shell and they just whizzed, shoooo (ph). Which brings back another thing. One of the other fears, worst fears in Hurtgen Forest was tree bursts, and they had what they called screaming Me-Mes and it's a psychological thing. It'll drive you nuts. These shells would just scream, but the tree bursts were designed that the minute they hit a tree branch above you, boom, they exploded and just bits of shrapnel all over hell. In fact, I had shrapnel in my arm that I never had come off until I was home five years. And I'd feel it and it would be sharp and before you know it a small little triangular piece would come out. It would work its way to the surface of your skin. They were horrible. Oh, those were the horrors in the forest and then it's--again it's so dark and so weird. God, so there we go. But we had a position and there was a hell of a minefield in between us. We didn't know too much about this because you can't detect them until something hits it. Then you know there's mines in there. And our guys, our engineers, hell, we didn't have enough of them to be everywhere, didn't get to this particular area and we had guns up on the front and we tried to get--they were radioing back or calling back by phone that they were getting short of ammo because they were getting hit pretty hard and we were trying to retaliate. So, okay. We sent a couple of boys up there. Jesus, they got clobbered. Hit mines no matter which direction they went they hit a mine. One lost a leg. And then the Germans had what they call castrator mines. Step on them and straight up. We lost one man. But after we lost a couple of men up through and then we didn't lose them all but they were wounded. One was a fatality. Why they still--they were getting lower and lower so... It's one of those things and you're properly half looped anyhow. You didn't give a damn anymore. You get--you get a very negative attitude after a while. What the hell, they've got to live, so let's go. So my buddy and I both started up there and we finally finagled a way you'd--what you did, you used to lay a tape down wherever you went and we found out where they, buddies before us went, and realized what the pattern was for the mines. So we figured out what the pattern from that point on up to where they were, we figured we could real gently like get between them and that's what we did. And that's putting it very brief. To scoot around them but mark them with this tape like they have the--you know like the police put up yellow tape only we used white. And marked where we thought they were and we did get a hole up through there where we can get men and then you get ammunition bearers, tell them and show them where the path laid. That's what that was all about there. And then the dam was after that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're being too modest.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're being modest about this actually.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: You don't talk to it too often.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: When you come home you never talk about it. It's only been recently that my kids have heard things that I never talked about. It's--it was a job to do and it's easy to get so you--I guess that's why when I first come home death didn't mean a thing to me. It was somebody died and somebody in my life, so what? Look at people that died like they did, these poor people up in New York. Jesus, what a horrible way to go. That's what it was over there. We saw it on Utah Beach, guys laying in the water. Geez.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you land on Utah Beach then? Is that right after, shortly after D Day?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: It was after D Day, yeah. It was after D Day before they got to Le Harve. So we were--let's see. We went over in September. D Day was in June. We were in September and that's when we went on--we went right about--that's an interesting point. And we laugh about it today, my buddy and I talk about it. He said do you realize when we left the United States we never touched English soil. Because they left us off on the--we went up the Irish Seas and landed in the Firth of Clyde in Scotland, Glasgow. We got off and they put us on a barge, took us to a train station which is right there, all concrete. And we laughed like hell when we saw those things and these trains, you know, the little beep, beep whistle and those high wheels and Holy Christ. Here was--we ended up later realizing it was a Scottish Flyer and that thing did just that. It flew. And we went from Glasgow, Scotland non stop to south--to England and got on the--a liberty ship to go across the Channel and never touched English soil. Always on concrete. We didn't have a day in England before we went across the Channel. But then when we come back, we come back on an LST. Jesus Christ. You talk about a floating cork on water. That is a floating cork. And it was one of those LSTs that we had with the narrow gauge railroad tracks in it that they put railroad cars in and shipped them to Europe and unloaded them, going to unload them at Cherbourg. So we waited until Cherbourg was taken and then they shipped us back to England on an LST. And that's the roughest piece of water that Christ ever put on this earth, that English Channel. Jesus, it was rough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: A lot of them. In fact, my one buddy is gone. He was from Indiana, Hammond, Indiana. These here were all in Camp Wheeler, Georgia. This is when you paid $5 for--this is in Reading. That was the place to be for servicemen in the Air Force. Goddamn. I was stationed on Chincoteague Island. That's where these are. See, they were worried about German submarines on the east coast and it happened. These--these were some of the pictures in Europe and this is--this is VE day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a good time on VE Day?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: You're Goddamn right we did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: These were all my relatives were all there. This is my buddy here. We were in the Air Force Cadet Program together. Come home and we--we went overseas together. And when we got overseas they transferred him to the Ninth Division, which what you got to remember, you read these stories about the Ninth Division done this or that, Eighth Army. We guys were all intermixed. Like I was--I was temporarily on temporary duty with A Company when that happened because that's where they needed a recon sergeant and we worked together. When we crossed the bridge they say the Ninth Division. Well, we were part of the Ninth Division when we crossed the bridge. We were one unit. But at any rate this was my buddy. He was real close to me. He come from Poland but he was a naturalized citizen. His mother and sister still lived in Poland at the time of the war. This was all still--somewhere in here we--I had a thing with all of the towns in Germany that we had been through.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a lot of letters from your wife when you were over there?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: A lot of them. See, this is my second wife. My first wife died and her husband died. Her husband was a POW. But that was all down in Virginia. This is in Maryland. They had snow in Maryland. That's how we slept in tents in Maryland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you mentioned--

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Here it is. These were all the towns and dates here that we were in Germany.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have trouble adjusting to civilian life after you got back?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Yes, you better believe it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nightmares, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Nightmares. If my first wife were living she would tell you I damn near choked her to death one night. I come home and she was shaking the living hell out of me and I had my hands around her neck and all she'll tell you I was saying I'll get you, you Goddamn Kraut, or else. And I was choking her and she got the strength enough to wham and woke me to my senses. Christ, I was scared to go to bed anymore. But, you know, when you see that for damn near two years it gets to you. It gets to you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you guys do anything to relieve the tension over there? Any entertainment or--

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: You know, that's a big joke. That's why I have no use for the Goddamn Red Cross, I'll be honest with you. The only Red Cross--people that had Red Cross people were the Air Force. They got the glory of it. We were--in that town of Helmerhausen when we were there, we had to haul water to where our guys were billeted in the field there. I went with my buddy just for a ride one morning. He had a jeep and we pulled a wagon, a trailer with a water tank on it. So we went to the air base there. There was a big air base, a fighter base, to get water and it was colder than hell. And whether you know it or not, we used to drive the jeeps with the windshields down with the canvas over them so it didn't reflect when you were driving in case they wanted to spot us from the air. They had a Red Cross canteen there. So colder than Billy hell. So we wanted to go in and get a cup of coffee. For Air Force personnel only. And we never got a cup of coffee and I--we never forgot it as long as we live and I never will. See, they didn't want to come where we were. We were up front, boy. Shit, they were fighting up there. People were dying from them bullets but the Air Forces, they all had Red Cross things. My buddy and I go around and around on this. He was with the 394th Bombardment Group, and don't get me wrong, they had a living hell, too. But at least they come home to a warm bed if they got home. I was kidding. I said you got a drink out of the deal. We didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: So but eventually then my dad got ahold of me when I come home. Boy, my language was horrible.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: I'm not proud of it but, boy, you got that way. Be happy today for tomorrow you may die. And, boy, he--I don't give a damn how old you are, you don't talk like that. Okay, okay, Dad. Of course, he was in the Sixth Division in World War 1 and he dreaded the day that my brother and I had went in service and all the things he never wanted us to see in the infantry because he was gassed. He only had one lung. But that's it. It's one of those things when you wouldn't take a million dollars for the experience you had but you wouldn't go through it again for a hundred million. No way. But again my father says the hell you say. He said--I come home and told him never again. I had all I wanted of it and he says well, you put a God darn gal up on Euclid Avenue in a short skirt and a military band and you'll be the first one to enlist. So there you go. But as I say, you know, my heart was in the Air Force. Geez, I love an airplane. I took the GI bill and I didn't want to go to college so I took flying lessons and got my license. Then along came a set of twins and that was the end of the flying. It's a rich man's play thing. But, you know, we--I think they--they brought out something the other night on television. It was in--well, in fact, it was on the History Channel. I don't know why the hell I go watch that stuff all over again. I never wanted to see "Private Ryan" but the guy said we really didn't know what we were really fighting for until we got to Dachau and Auschwitz and saw the results of the tyranny of Nazism. Then we finally--this is what you were fighting for. And, boy, here we are going through the same damn thing. We're getting hit with our own technology. But one other thing I would like to make clear. There is nothing else in life, nothing you can--no organization you can belong to that there is the bond between men that you have in service. One guy will help another like you never had before and, you know, even though I'm not as active in the Legion as I used to be, I used to be I wouldn't miss a meeting but I haven't been very active in the Legion. I got involved over here in the Kiwanis Club and it's strictly a business club and I--you don't have any little--little nit--nitpicking stuff. It's business and it's over with and I like it. So I--but I'm still a member and I'll always be a member because I love the guys that are in it. That Jim Warner is as fine a guy and so is Frank and all the rest of them. I would go to bat for them any time. In fact, we're going to get together Sunday night for this big shindig at the fairgrounds for a memorial. But as I say again there's no bond like any--you hear of one of your buddies and, of course, mine are--they're getting thin, boy. And you hear from them and you go to any length to see them or meet them. And like George and I and our wives, we get together next Tuesday and we'll end up at the restaurant about 11:30 and walk out of there about 3 or 3:30. But they don't care. And you relive the whole thing over again. And his wife was an Army nurse. Then when my brother was here from Arkansas, he lives in Arkansas, he went with us one day and he was with the Fourth Armored. And he was--one time we were within 16 miles of each other and never knew it. But it's--it's--it's such a bond. I think it's because you knew you had somebody to talk to that was on the same grounds as you were. You knew you could--you had to depend on him and he had to depend on you. And like the incident I told you about the Black. That was--that was something else. I had one other incident. This happened with a white man. I'm Catholic, born and raised Catholic. Not that it really matters at all, but we had a Catholic chaplain in our outfit, Father Horn. Before we went into combat he used to have mass on the Jeep, hood of a Jeep. So our guys included Hank +++ and they'd go to mass. And then I come back and you always had a smart ass buddy. You always had to have clowns. That's what keeps you going. And he says boy, he says you bunch of hypocrites. He says that's a bunch of bullshit, that church business. He says I'm an atheist and proud of it. Okay. I says okay. You be what you want to be, I'll be what I am. What the hell. I don't hold that against anybody. They can be what they want to be. But he was hit and I seen him laying there and he's hollering oh, my God, help me, oh, my God, help me. And I never should have done it but I did it, and I still think of it to this day. I says what the hell are you asking God to help you for? I said you just got through telling me 15 minutes ago that there is no God. Now you're hollering God help me. So I got a medic and took care of it. He went to the hospital and I never saw him after that. I really don't know whatever happened to him. But those are incidental things. I got another book over here. It's called "At Ease". It's all about little incidents like that, not the battles that you fought but little incidents, things that happened. You know, like the student that was taken -- was on a fly out of Randolph Field in Texas forgot to hook his seatbelt and the instructor turned him upside down and he fell out, stuff like that. Geez.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he have a parachute?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Oh, yeah. That was a must. You had to have a parachute. But it goes on to say it's a lesson the kid never forgot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Those are actually the stories I'm very interested in because I know enough about history and I'm always interested in those little stories like that.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: This was another scare, the bridge. That's where we had the first encounter with the German jets. And our--I don't know if you know it but anti-aircraft fire is set up on a triangular system. And the timing is set up that the gun fires so many leads ahead of the aircraft so that they run into each other. But when the jets come over they were so damn fast we were ten airplanes behind them but we didn't know what we were--we never had a jet before. We listened to the sound and didn't know what the hell they were. And then they--they didn't have the pilots that were trained and they--their pilots couldn't cope with them either. They were--they were--their bombing was atrocious.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Thank God it was because they missed the bridge all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't know how to fly those things, did they?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: No, they didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A handful of test pilots maybe.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Geez. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: +++ pilots anyway at that point.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: But basically that's about all. It took me--the standing joke is it took me 12 months to get transferred from the Infantry to the Air Force and was I happy, and it took me three minutes to get put back to the ground forces. And when we left Albright College--I've been up to Albright College a couple of times since. When we left that college Reading, Pennsylvania had two weeks of the biggest bunch of drunks they ever had in their life but they were sympathetic with us. Geez. It's just that all of us knew what we were going back to. Now, if we had never been in the Infantry before it would have been different, but we got out of the Infantry because we hated it. Sleeping on the damn ground in a pup tent and cleaning a rifle. That's another thing. When I got out of service I swore to Christ, I was never going to clean or shoot another rifle as long as I did and I--lived and I haven't. I gigged so many--Christ, take you out on a rifle range all day long in sand and then march you five miles home and then you've got 15 minutes for 66 guys to get cleaned up and stand a retreat and then get gigford (ph) sand on your rifle. That used to burn me. Christ, you had no time. But that was war and so that turned me off. I wouldn't--even fireworks shake me up. I don't go for fireworks. So there we are.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: My dad went sort of the same route. Well, pretty much the same route. He was in the Infantry for a short while, got into the ASTP, wanted to be a flier.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Went into the Cadet program and went to University of Wyoming and Nebraska, and then the word came down if you were in the Infantry before you're back in the Infantry now.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Yeah, see. That--I was on CQ that night up at Albright and we're just getting ready to change the guard and this telegram come in. So I opened it and I read that thing, Holy Christ. I was ready to get drunk that night and it was a theological college. There wasn't anything around there. But we survived for some reason. The good Lord let me here. I must have a job to do yet. So I just am a month short of five years, four years in the service, 47 weeks, months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had enough points.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: And, you know, when you--your guys and most of the other guys I went in it was a matter of none of us had never been--ever traveled you know. Hell, I never was on a train before in my life.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: And it was an experience. But I'll say this for the military. I don't care how miserable it might have been and all this, but I'll tell you something. The service made more men out of boys in a hell of a hurry than any other thing in this life. And the things that are laughable now. Somebody stole my raincoat at Camp Wheeler. So I went to the old man and told him, the first sergeant, you know, First Sergeant, what am I supposed to do? You know, scared to hell because I'm going to have to pay for that $21 a month. Holy Christ. He said well, steal it from somebody else. I thought Holy Christ, this is the Army? Oh, Jesus. But got the first--my first check $21 a month and then they take $6 out for laundry, canteen checks. Christ, I had about $5 left to go to the next month. Then I got a raise of PFC and another raise for corporal and then I had the sergeant and then oversees pay and then--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you get as a PFC?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: PFC we got--what was it? 33 I think it was. 21 to 30--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is E-5 the same as corporal?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: No. That would be a tech. That would be a corporal, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the same pay rate I assume?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So I'm trying to find out what my dad made. What did my dad make as a tech five then?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: A tech five. I was making 66 as a buck sergeant and I think a tech five was--in those days was I think around 77 and then you got I think it was $10 for overseas pay, this kind of stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was in the gravy.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, what's the tech five? How does that differ from corporal?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Well, it's a technical thing. It's what you--a specific job. That's the big thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So his job as a lead scout, for instance, that would be a tech five?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Right, that would be different. He would have been a scout leader. See, like mine was a tech sergeant mine and mine is just a buck sergeant. But it was just reconnaissance see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And the reconnaissance?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Yes. Yeah. See.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As a forward observer?

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Yes. Well, you know, what we get is, we get a magazine from the division every quarterly, three quarter or every quarter, and have battlefield tours and they go over there every two years. And the guys come back and they say there's certain areas they have changed drastically and others he said there's still some of the wreckage still there. They've left it set. Now, back to Hurtgen Forest. George was telling me, he went over there with his wife the last time which was two years ago, and he said there's areas in Hurtgen Forest where you still cannot go because they're still cleaning mines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: Three hundred people a year are injured or killed from buried ammos in the Hurtgen Forest area. It's growing up with undergrowth and then he said they'll go in to develop it and a bulldozer will hit a bomb that didn't explode or something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Albert Boehnlein
sp.p: It's still a tragic thing. And he said they have everything marked off in sections that has been cleaned and he says we're still paying a big price to have that cleared. And it was real interesting to show you the bond. We went to Louisville, Kentucky last September for our convention. We have it every two years. We're going to go this coming year, we're going to Pittsburgh. And we had three families from the Netherlands, Belgium and Holland come over that were friends of ours and one fellow was from Germany and he was with the 274th Volksgenader, the Volks folks division and grenadiers, and he also got up, the German, and said he wanted to come over himself and personally thank us for the way we treated them as POWs and so forth. That we were humane. And he, too, said I don't know why I can look at you and be my friend and you can look at me and we don't have to shoot each other. And back to the Netherlands. Three generations are still keeping flowers on American graves over there because they wanted to come over and thank us for their freedom. We gave them freedom that they never would have had otherwise. And that's really--it's really gratifying. It's so good to talk to them. Yep.
